strengths: The manuscript is clearly organized and visually polished, with readable pseudocode, extensive qualitative results, and a useful appendix containing proofs, hyperparameters, runtime measurements, failure cases, and implementation details. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/1d39721a859d4aeb8bc89f3c0babf37b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Quantized expectation through the lookup-free codebook and posterior-confidence-based anchored remasking form an interesting, plausibly useful combination for adapting masked discrete diffusion models without updating the denoiser.

The evaluation covers several linear and nonlinear inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet. The identical-prior comparison in Table 5 is especially valuable: under the same VQ-Diffusion prior and optimization budget, APS improves PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over G2D2.

The paper reports computational costs, memory, hyperparameter sensitivity, tokenizer and backbone limitations, and concrete failure cases. Its ethics discussion appropriately warns that posterior reconstructions are plausible samples rather than factual recovery and identifies risks in forensic use and information leakage.

The broader direction is significant: a reliable training-free posterior method for discrete multimodal foundation models could avoid denoiser backpropagation and extend inverse-problem techniques beyond continuous diffusion.
weaknesses: The central theoretical construction is not sound as written. Equation 6 and Theorem A.1 define each reverse transition as q(z_s^l|z_t,x_phi(z_t)) q(y|x_phi(z_t)). The likelihood is a scalar independent of z_s^l, so the expression is not normalized; multiplying it across L positions compounds the same scalar L times. If normalized, that scalar cancels and produces the unconditional transition. Consequently, p_phi(x,z_0:1|y) is not established as a probability distribution, and the Jensen/variational derivations in Theorems 3.1, 3.2, A.1, and A.2 do not justify the claimed posterior bound.

The implemented objective is only heuristically connected to those theorems. Equation 7 replaces the unknown ground-truth token x with the pretrained prediction x_theta, while quantization is differentiated using a straight-through estimator. Neither substitution preserves the stated upper bound. The resulting optimize-and-remask algorithm is not shown to have q(x|y) as a stationary or limiting distribution, so calling it principled posterior sampling is unsupported.

The main comparison is confounded by the resolution protocol. Appendix B.1.3 says a 256x256 ground-truth image is first upsampled to 512x512 or 1024x1024, corrupted at that resolution, reconstructed, and then downsampled for scoring. For 4x super-resolution this supplies a 128x128 or 256x256 measurement, rather than the 64x64 measurement obtained by corrupting the native benchmark image; blur kernels likewise change their physical scale. Unless every baseline receives exactly the same resulting measurement, APS—especially APS-L—is solving an easier, different inverse problem. This undermines the headline gains in Table 1.

The evidence does not adequately isolate the two claimed innovations. Figure 6 is a qualitative ablation on one image, while the only controlled quantitative comparison in Table 5 changes quantized expectation, anchored remasking, and the perceptual loss together. Quantitative ablations for each component, multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates, and measurement-consistency or posterior-calibration tests are absent.

Several empirical claims are overstated. Standard APS is substantially behind DAPS on all four Table 1 settings and often has worse LPIPS than DPS or PSLD in Table 2; the strongest numbers mainly come from the questionable APS-L protocol. In stylization, APS improves over its MMaDA backbone but trails RB-Modulation markedly on ImageReward and DINO. Sample counts and uncertainty are not reported for the stylization evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the reproducibility statement. No release of the APS modifications is identified; UpdateState and the exact threshold schedule are underspecified; Algorithm 1 lists lambda_e but uses lambda_p and lambda_pp; and Table 6's resolution labels are difficult to reconcile with the stated native-resolution protocol. The 100K-image garment fine-tuning lacks optimizer, duration, split, and dataset-construction details, while the main text presents that experiment near claims of training-free operation.

The limitations and ethics sections are constructive, but they omit the most consequential limitations: the unnormalized theoretical kernel, the heuristic nature of the supposed posterior approximation, and the potentially easier high-resolution corruption protocol. These issues are fundamental enough that the otherwise promising algorithmic and empirical contribution is not currently reliable for acceptance.

The experimental scope is broad, covering two datasets, several linear and nonlinear inverse problems, stylization, and editing. The same-prior comparison against G2D2 in Table 5 is particularly useful and shows empirical gains at matched compute.
The paper reports runtime and memory, gives pseudocode and principal hyperparameters, and includes a 1,000-image FFHQ super-resolution evaluation.
The limitations and ethics discussions appropriately acknowledge hallucinated reconstruction details, forensic misuse, tokenizer/backbone limitations, information leakage, and stylization failures.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is fundamentally unsound. Equation (6) defines a reverse transition as q(z_s|z_t,x_phi(z_t)) q(y|x_phi(z_t)) without a normalizing constant. This does not sum to one and therefore is not a Markov kernel, so the joint p_phi used in the Jensen/ELBO derivation is not a probability distribution. If normalized over z_s, the likelihood factor—being independent of z_s—cancels completely. Consequently, Theorems 3.1/3.2 and their claimed likelihood tilting do not follow.

Even setting that error aside, the implemented method is not derived from the stated bound. Equation (7) replaces the unavailable ground-truth token with the denoiser prediction without proving that the result remains a bound, while Algorithm 1 optimizes L1 plus VGG perceptual loss rather than the Gaussian likelihood used in the theory and normally sets the stated prior-preservation coefficient to zero. Thus the theory does not support the actual algorithm.

The work does not establish that APS is a posterior sampler. The procedure optimizes logits, quantizes their expectation, and commits tokens, but the paper provides no stationarity, convergence, posterior-consistency, or approximation result for this process. Evaluation uses point-reconstruction metrics only; there are no tests of posterior diversity, coverage, calibration, or uncertainty, nor meaningful multiple-sample analysis.

The empirical claims are overstated. In Table 2, APS has worse LPIPS than DPS on FFHQ inpainting (0.304 vs. 0.203), motion deblurring (0.317 vs. 0.246), and HDR (0.282 vs. 0.264), among other losses, despite prose claiming consistent superiority. Standard APS also trails strong continuous methods on several Table 1 settings; many headline gains require APS-L, which takes 484 seconds and 51.8 GiB per image.

The main component ablation is only one qualitative example. Table 5 compares the complete method—including perceptual loss—against G2D2, so it does not isolate quantized expectation or anchored remasking. There are no quantitative removals, uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or statistical tests. Most principal tables use only 100 images.

Comparison fairness is difficult to assess: methods use different priors, native resolutions, compute budgets, and GPUs. APS-L first upsamples a 256×256 target, applies the degradation at 1024×1024, reconstructs there, and downsamples for scoring; this changes the inverse problem and can itself improve distortion metrics. Runtime rows mix copied A6000 measurements with new A100 measurements.

The claimed novelty of anchored remasking is not convincingly distinguished from standard confidence remasking. Both compute per-token confidence from denoiser outputs conditioned on the full sequence; calling the proposed score 'joint' does not make the selection rule joint. Quantized expectation mainly combines expected embeddings, lookup-free quantization, and a straight-through estimator, all established ingredients.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the statement. No implementation is supplied or explicitly committed for release; UpdateState and the exact threshold schedule are underspecified; seeds and many task-specific choices are absent; and Algorithm 1 inconsistently lists lambda_e while using lambda_pp. The 100K-image fine-tuning for block inpainting lacks optimizer, schedule, epochs, split, and compute details.

The paper repeatedly presents the approach as training-free, yet the high-resolution text-guided inpainting experiment fine-tunes MMaDA on 100K fashion images using the proposed training objective. This important qualification appears only in the appendix and undermines the framing of the showcased editing result. Overall, the invalid core theory and lack of evidence for posterior sampling are fundamental deficiencies, despite a potentially useful restoration heuristic.

strengths: Originality: Quantized expectation through lookup-free quantization and posterior-confidence-based anchored remasking form an interesting adaptation of gradient guidance to masked discrete diffusion. The same-prior, same-compute comparison with G2D2 in Table 5 helps isolate some algorithmic benefit.

Significance: Training-free use of discrete diffusion foundation models for inverse problems is timely and potentially useful, particularly if it can reduce the number of reverse steps and avoid backpropagation through an 8B-parameter denoiser.

Empirical breadth: The manuscript studies FFHQ and ImageNet, multiple linear and nonlinear operators, stylization, high-resolution inference, runtime, and failure cases. APS generally improves over the discrete baselines on the principal super-resolution and deblurring benchmarks.

Presentation: The paper is visually polished and largely well organized. The algorithm, implementation settings, runtime measurements, and high-level roles of the two proposed components are explained clearly.

Limitations and ethics: The discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on tokenizer and backbone quality, out-of-distribution failures, dual-use risks, and—importantly—that inverse-problem outputs are plausible posterior reconstructions rather than factual recovery suitable for forensic identification.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive theoretical issue: Equation (6) defines each reverse transition as q(z_s^l|z_t^l,x_phi(z_t)) q(y|x_phi(z_t)). This is not normalized as a categorical distribution. Moreover, the likelihood factor is independent of z_s^l, so normalizing the transition would cancel it and provide no likelihood guidance. The outer product over L coordinates also repeats the same global likelihood L times. Consequently, the joint distribution used in Theorems 3.1/A.1 is generally not a probability distribution, invalidating the Jensen/KL derivations and the claimed posterior-likelihood bounds. This is not a minor notation omission because the implemented guidance does not follow from a valid tilted transition.

The passage from Theorem 3.2 to Equation (7) substitutes the unknown ground-truth token with the pretrained model prediction without establishing that the resulting expression remains an upper bound or approximates the desired posterior. The practical algorithm then omits the derived adaptation term by setting the prior-preservation coefficient to zero and replaces the assumed Gaussian log-likelihood with L1 plus VGG perceptual losses. Thus, the theory does not support the actual method.

The method is called a posterior sampler, but evaluation only measures point-reconstruction quality. There is no assessment of posterior calibration, conditional sample diversity, uncertainty, coverage, or convergence/stationarity. With per-step logit optimization, straight-through quantization, and deterministic confidence selection, APS is closer to a guided reconstruction heuristic unless its distributional validity is demonstrated.

The headline comparisons are potentially confounded by resolution and measurement information. APS first upsamples 256×256 ground truth to 512×512 or 1024×1024, applies the forward operator there, and downsamples the reconstruction for evaluation. For 4× super-resolution, this exposes measurements at 128×128 or 256×256 rather than the conventional 64×64 measurement of a 256×256 target. The paper does not provide a controlled comparison showing that baselines receive equivalent observations. APS-L's strongest gains therefore cannot be confidently attributed to the sampling algorithm.

The empirical claims are overstated. In Table 2, APS/APS-L often has worse LPIPS than DPS for FFHQ inpainting, motion deblurring, and HDR, and for ImageNet inpainting and nonlinear deblurring. In Table 1, standard APS is substantially worse than DAPS on LPIPS throughout. Runtime comparisons also mix A6000 and A100 measurements and different priors, step counts, and resolutions.

Component evidence is inadequate: the principal ablation in Figure 6 is a single qualitative example, with no quantitative factorial ablation separating quantized expectation, anchored remasking, perceptual loss, resolution scaling, and base-prior effects. Results are mostly based on only 100 images, without repeated seeds, variability estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful pseudocode and several hyperparameters. The APS implementation is not released; the exact threshold schedule and UpdateState behavior, VGG features, random seeds, evaluation generation protocol, and several task-specific choices are insufficiently specified. The text-guided inpainting experiment additionally fine-tunes on 100K fashion images but gives no precise dataset split, license/provenance details, training configuration, or quantitative evaluation, and it conflicts with the broad training-free framing.

Presentation is weakened by inconsistencies such as describing a qualitative-only ablation as systematic, claiming all experiment parameters are specified when key details are absent, and presenting the fine-tuned block-inpainting application alongside training-free claims without clearly separating the settings. The core heuristic is promising, but the invalid theoretical foundation and confounded evidence prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: Quantized expectation combined with measurement-aware remasking is a useful approach to extending gradient-guided inverse-problem methods to masked discrete diffusion, particularly lookup-free binary tokenizers.

Soundness: The identical-prior experiment in Table 7 is valuable: using VQ-Diffusion with matched sampling/optimization budgets, APS improves PSNR from 25.46 to 26.80, SSIM from 0.720 to 0.759, and LPIPS from 0.349 to 0.310 relative to a perceptual-loss-enhanced G2D2 baseline. The measurement-noise sweep also shows consistent gains.

Significance: The experiments cover FFHQ and ImageNet, several linear and nonlinear operators, stylization, and language generation. Runtime and memory are reported, and the 15-step MMaDA implementation appears practically useful despite its inner optimization.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally polished and well organized, with readable figures, pseudocode, implementation details, qualitative failure cases, and a helpful discussion of approximate rather than asymptotically exact sampling.

Reproducibility/ethics: Public datasets and backbone implementations are identified, degradation parameters and major optimizer settings are supplied, and the impact statement appropriately warns that plausible posterior reconstructions must not be treated as factual evidence. weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed theoretical grounding does not carry through to the implemented algorithm. Equation 8 replaces the log-ratio term of Equation 7 with a log inner product without establishing a bound or controlled approximation. More importantly, Algorithm 1 optimizes only reconstruction plus perceptual loss and omits Equation 8's prior-alignment term altogether. It also declares an entropy coefficient that never appears in the algorithm. The generic variational bound therefore provides little support for the actual sampler.

Soundness/evaluation fairness: Most headline comparisons use different priors and, more seriously, different effective inverse problems. APS upsamples each 256x256 ground truth to 512x512 or 1024x1024 before applying the operator, whereas native-resolution baselines operate on the original image. For 4x super-resolution, this gives APS measurements of size 128x128 or 256x256 rather than the baseline's 64x64 measurement, potentially exposing substantially more information. Downsampling the final reconstruction does not make these observation models equivalent. Consequently, Tables 1–2 do not support the broad superiority claims; the fairer same-prior Table 7 is much narrower and has smaller gains.

The anchored-remasking justification is overstated. Both the base denoiser's per-token probabilities and the optimized probabilities are conditioned on the full sequence; calling the latter a joint posterior while characterizing standard confidence as non-contextual is not technically persuasive. The paper provides only a qualitative component ablation in Figure 6, with no quantitative comparison isolating anchored remasking from quantized expectation.

Several conclusions are selective. In Table 2, APS is worse than continuous baselines on LPIPS for many settings, including both random-inpainting datasets and FFHQ motion deblurring. In stylization, APS improves MMaDA but is well behind RB-Modulation on ImageReward and several continuous methods on DINO. DDRM is also far faster than APS in Table 8, contrary to broad efficiency rhetoric.

The language experiment is insufficient to establish generalization: it contains only 20 prompts generated by Qwen2.5, optimizes a Qwen3-0.6B score, and evaluates with another Qwen-family model, with no human evaluation, uncertainty, or independent standard benchmark. The mechanism for differentiating through a reward model that consumes discrete text is not specified well enough to reproduce the reported result.

Empirical uncertainty is absent: results generally use 100 images, but there are no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests. Hyperparameter selection appears to use the same benchmark sets later reported, and the quantitative ablations do not separately test all proposed components.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the statement in Appendix C.11. The manuscript does not release its modifications, omits random seeds and some exact evaluation/scoring details, and contains inconsistencies between the prose loss, Equation 8, and Algorithm 1. These gaps would make independent reproduction difficult.

Overall, the core idea is promising and the controlled comparison indicates genuine merit, but the theoretical-to-algorithm gap and confounded headline evaluation prevent the central claims from being considered reliably supported. A revision should evaluate all methods under identical observation operators and priors, align the implemented objective with the theory, and provide quantitative component ablations and stronger statistical evaluation.

strengths: Originality/significance: Combining expected LFQ codebook embeddings with straight-through optimization and posterior-confidence remasking is a plausible practical approach to controlled masked-diffusion inference. The ability to reuse a multimodal discrete model across restoration and stylization tasks could be useful.

Empirical breadth: The paper considers FFHQ and ImageNet, several linear and nonlinear operators, reference-based stylization, and language generation. The same-prior comparison with G2D2 in Table 7, optimization-step study in Table 6, noise study in Table 9, and runtime/memory reporting are valuable additions.

Presentation: The main algorithm is understandable, and the appendix provides pseudocode, operator settings, a hyperparameter sweep, complexity discussion, failure cases, and an honest statement that APS is biased rather than an asymptotically exact posterior sampler.

Limitations and ethics are treated responsibly. The paper explicitly discusses dependence on tokenizer/backbone quality, out-of-distribution stylization failures, hallucination risks in inverse problems, and unsuitable forensic or identity-verification uses. weaknesses: Soundness: The implemented algorithm does not optimize the theoretically derived surrogate. Equation 8 contains a prior/adaptation term tying the optimized distribution to the denoiser, whereas Algorithm 1 uses only reconstruction plus perceptual loss. The prose additionally mentions an entropy term and lists its coefficient as tunable, but Algorithm 1 omits it. The Gaussian likelihood underlying the derivation is also replaced by L1 and VGG losses. Consequently, the generic variational bounds do not substantiate the actual APS procedure or its description as theoretically grounded.

The principal cross-method inverse-problem comparisons are not controlled. APS first upsamples each 256x256 ground-truth image to the model's 512x512 or 1024x1024 native resolution, applies the corruption there, and then downsamples its reconstruction for evaluation. For 4x super-resolution, APS-L therefore receives a 256x256 measurement derived from an upsampled image, while a conventional 256x256 benchmark method receives a 64x64 measurement. This can preserve substantially more information and makes Table 1's APS/APS-L comparison, especially the claimed gains from APS-L, difficult to interpret as an algorithmic improvement.

The component evidence is inadequate. Figure 6 is a single qualitative trajectory; there is no quantitative factorial ablation separating quantized expectation, anchored remasking, perceptual loss, backbone, and resolution. Table 7 controls the prior only for FFHQ super-resolution and attributes the aggregate gain to several changes simultaneously. Thus, the two claimed innovations are not individually established.

The conceptual account of anchored remasking is overstated. The optimized distribution remains a product of token-wise categorical marginals. Saying it captures a joint relationship merely because its logits depend on the full context does not distinguish it from the base denoiser, whose per-token confidences also depend on the full sequence. The proposed operation appears closer to confidence remasking after test-time logit optimization than to demonstrated joint sampling.

Several empirical conclusions exceed the results. In Table 2, APS is often worse than DPS or PSLD on LPIPS and sometimes PSNR; nonlinear tasks omit strong alternatives, and no discrete baseline is evaluated there. Stylization trails RB-Modulation substantially on ImageReward and DINO. Accordingly, broad claims of superiority or state-of-the-art posterior sampling are not supported consistently.

The language experiment is too small to support generalization claims: it uses only 20 machine-generated, mostly simple personal-writing prompts, with no human evaluation, repeated runs, uncertainty, or established benchmark. The reward model and judge are differently sized models from the same Qwen family, leaving correlated evaluation and reward-hacking concerns. Calling this question answering is also misleading because many prompts are creative writing or formatting tasks.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the detailed appendix. APS code is not supplied, and important details such as random seeds, stochastic repetitions, exact threshold/update-state implementation, entropy regularization, some checkpoint/configuration choices, and stylization evaluation sample counts are absent or inconsistent. Most reported metrics have neither variability nor confidence intervals and are based on only 100 images.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: expected codebook embeddings, straight-through estimators, test-time likelihood optimization, and confidence-based remasking are established ingredients. The paper does not provide sufficiently controlled evidence or theory showing that their particular combination yields a fundamentally new posterior-sampling principle. These central evidential and theory-to-implementation gaps prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality: APS combines quantized expectations with posterior-informed remasking in a novel and practically useful way. Updating the full categorical distribution through expected codebook embeddings is a sensible approach to obtaining gradient-like guidance for discrete visual tokens.

Soundness: The strongest evidence is the controlled same-prior comparison in Table 7. With identical VQ-Diffusion priors and compute budgets, APS improves G2D2 from 25.46 to 26.80 PSNR, 0.720 to 0.759 SSIM, and 0.349 to 0.310 LPIPS. This substantially reduces concern that the headline gains arise solely from using the stronger MMaDA backbone.

The inverse-problem evaluation is broad, covering FFHQ and ImageNet, multiple linear and nonlinear operators, measurement-noise sweeps, and both perceptual and distortion metrics. The 1,000-image FFHQ super-resolution result also supports the main trend beyond the default 100-image evaluation.

Significance: Avoiding backpropagation through the large denoiser is practically valuable. The reported 15-step MMaDA implementation is substantially faster than several continuous posterior samplers, while the method is applicable to pretrained discrete diffusion models without task-specific model training.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized, with pseudocode, extensive implementation details, complexity discussion, qualitative trajectories, failure cases, and an honest acknowledgment that APS produces biased approximate rather than asymptotically exact posterior samples.

The limitations and impact discussions are appropriate. In particular, the paper explicitly warns that perceptually plausible reconstructions are not evidentiary recovery of the original signal and discusses tokenizer, backbone, and out-of-distribution style limitations without overstating safety.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theoretical objective and implemented algorithm are insufficiently aligned. Equation 8 contains an explicit prior-correlation term and is derived using a Gaussian likelihood, whereas Algorithm 1 optimizes only reconstruction plus perceptual loss; the surrounding text additionally mentions an entropy term that is absent from the pseudocode. The experiments use L1 and VGG losses rather than the likelihood assumed by the derivation. Consequently, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 motivate a family of likelihood-tilted chains but do not directly establish that the evaluated APS algorithm optimizes the stated bound or approximates the desired posterior well.

The anchored-remasking justification is overstated. Both the base and adapted per-token probabilities are conditioned on the entire partially decoded sequence, so the claim that APS uniquely captures joint token relations whereas standard confidence is only per-token is not established. The component ablation in Figure 6 is mainly one qualitative trajectory; a quantitative factorial ablation separating quantized expectation, posterior-based remasking, prior regularization, and perceptual loss is needed.

The headline empirical claims are broader than the results. In Table 2, APS often has worse LPIPS than DPS and PSLD—for example, on random inpainting for both datasets and FFHQ motion deblurring—and APS-L is not uniformly better than APS. Thus the work is strong among discrete samplers on the principal SR/deblurring benchmarks, but it does not consistently dominate continuous methods across general inverse problems.

Several comparisons confound algorithm, backbone, native resolution, and compute. APS/APS-L apply the corruption after upsampling inputs to 512 or 1024 pixels and then downsample outputs for evaluation, whereas many baselines use different priors and native resolutions. The identical-prior experiment is persuasive but is limited to one task, dataset, and prior; analogous controlled comparisons on ImageNet, nonlinear tasks, and masked diffusion would materially strengthen the conclusions.

The language and stylization extensions are preliminary. Question answering uses only 20 model-generated prompts, a Qwen reward model and a larger judge from the same model family, with no human evaluation, repeated generations, uncertainty, or detailed judging protocol. Stylization likewise lacks sample counts, uncertainty, and human preference evaluation. These studies demonstrate feasibility rather than robust generality.

Reproducibility is only moderate despite the detailed appendix. The paper does not provide an APS code release, random seeds, uncertainty estimates, exact threshold schedule values, complete loss specification consistent with Algorithm 1, or sufficient details about the number of samples and selection protocol for stylization and language experiments. The missing PSLD source link and comparisons measured on different GPU types further complicate replication.

Presentation has a few consequential inconsistencies: the complexity discussion initially characterizes the exact expectation in ways that mix token-wise and joint marginalizations, the algorithm declares an entropy coefficient without using it, and the high-resolution fashion experiment fine-tunes the backbone despite being presented alongside the paper's training-free applications. These issues should be corrected or clearly scoped.
